Needful
nēd'fu̇l
adj. (necessary; requisite; that which is wanted or required)
Old English nied, necessity, compulsion, with the suffix -ful. The Greek in Luke 10:42 is chreia, need — the same word Paul uses of God supplying all your need according to His riches.

Biblical Definition

The word's great occurrence is in a kitchen. Martha is cumbered about much serving and complains that her sister has left her to serve alone, and the answer is not a rebuke of hospitality but a correction of measure: “But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luk 10:42). Many things were being done that afternoon and one of them was necessary. Jude uses the word of a change of subject forced upon him: he had intended to write of the common salvation, but “it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). The pleasant letter was set aside for the urgent one. Paul weighs his own life by it, saying that to depart and be with Christ is far better, “Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you” (Php 1:24) — a man reckoning his own death against a congregation's need and deciding by theirs. James turns it toward the poor: a word of blessing that withholds the things needful to the body profits nothing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines needful as necessary, as supply to a want; requisite; things needful for the body.

expand to see more

NEEDFUL, a. Necessary, as supply to a want; requisite.

All things needful for defense abound.

2. Needy; in want; distressful.

Key Scripture

Luk 10:42 — "But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her."

Php 1:24 — "Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you."

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Modern Corruption

Therapeutic culture has made my needs the governing category of moral reasoning, so that a duty is weighed by whether it meets them; Scripture uses the word to rank duties, and ranks the hearing of Christ first.

expand to see more

The modern usage runs the word inward. A man's needs become the fixed point around which relationships, work, and church membership are arranged, and an obligation that fails to serve them is judged unreasonable by that fact alone. Scripture's uses run the other way in every instance. Paul asks what is needful for you and stays alive for it. Jude asks what is needful for the churches and writes the letter he had not planned. James asks what is needful to the body of a brother who is naked and destitute, and makes the answer a test of whether faith is alive. Even the Lord's word to Martha, which is the one text that does concern the hearer's own good, defines that good as sitting at another's feet to hear his word. What the passage does not do is what it is often made to do, namely disparage the serving. The Lord does not tell Martha to stop cooking; He tells her she is careful and troubled about many things when one is needful, and the disorder is in the ranking, not in the work. A Christian who has genuinely put the one thing first will not serve less; he will serve without being cumbered.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek chreia (G5532), need, necessity; anagkaios (G316), necessary, indispensable; epanagke, of necessity, in the decree of Acts 15.

expand to see more

Greek chreia (G5532) — need, necessity, want; one thing is needful, and God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory; Luke 10:42, Philippians 4:19.

Greek anagkaios (G316) — necessary, indispensable; Paul's abiding in the flesh more needful for the Philippians than his own departure; Philippians 1:24.

Greek anagke (G318) — constraint, necessity; Jude's compulsion to write of contending for the faith instead of the common salvation; Jude 3.

Usage

"“One thing is needful” — the disorder is in the ranking, not in the serving."

"“To abide in the flesh is more needful for you” — a man deciding by his congregation's need."

"“It was needful for me to write unto you... earnestly contend for the faith” — the urgent letter displacing the pleasant one."
